item.title: Supersolid created at room temperature
item.description: An international team created a supersolid in an exciton-polariton Bose-Einstein condensate at room temperature, in liquid-crystal microcavities that work at up to about 60°C (140°F) with no cryogenic fridge. With each laser pulse the condensate's stripes reformed in slightly different places, evidence of spontaneous symmetry breaking rather than an artefact of the cavity.

item.title: Big Idea: The Twin Earth Thought Experiment — Daily Learning
item.description: In Hilary Putnam's 1975 paper, imagine a planet exactly like Earth, where the clear liquid everyone calls “water” is not H2O but a different chemical, XYZ, and where you and your Twin Earth double are molecule-for-molecule identical inside, with the same thoughts about “water” in your heads before anyone knew the chemistry in 1750. Putnam argued you still are not referring to the same thing,…
item.content:encoded: In Hilary Putnam's 1975 paper, imagine a planet exactly like Earth, where the clear liquid everyone calls “water” is not H2O but a different chemical, XYZ, and where you and your Twin Earth double are molecule-for-molecule identical inside, with the same thoughts about “water” in your heads before anyone knew the chemistry in 1750. Putnam argued you still are not referring to the same thing, because your “water” picks out H2O and theirs picks out XYZ, so meaning is not just in the head, and that raises whether a mind, or a machine trained only on text, could ever mean what we mean.

item.title: Statistics: The Lindley Paradox — Daily Learning
item.description: Flip a coin 100,000 times and get 50,400 heads, and the test calls the result significant at p ≈ 0.01 even though the rate is only 50.4%. A Bayesian reading of those same flips says they fit a fair coin far better than any specific biased alternative, so with samples that large a p-value alone can mislead you.

item.title: Word of the Day: zugzwang — Daily Learning
item.description: Zugzwang (TSOOK-tsvahng) is a noun from German Zug, move, and Zwang, compulsion, naming a chess position where you must move but every legal move worsens your position. In the negotiation, she was in zugzwang: conceding on price would cost her margin, walking away would cost her the client, and stalling would cost her trust.

item.title: Statistics: Benford's Law — Daily Learning
item.description: In many real-world datasets, 1 is the leading digit about 30% of the time and 9 only about 5%, far from the roughly 11% each you would expect if digits were random. That uneven falloff is a tripwire for made-up numbers.

item.title: Big Idea: The Sleeping Beauty Problem — Daily Learning
item.description: On Sunday Beauty is put to sleep, and a fair coin decides whether she wakes on Monday only or on Monday and Tuesday with her memory erased, so she never knows which day it is or whether she has woken before. The Sleeping Beauty problem still splits Bayesians between 1/2 and 1/3, over what counts as evidence when you are the one being sampled.

item.title: Word of the Day: aporia — Daily Learning
item.description: Aporia (uh-POR-ee-uh) is a noun from Greek a-poros, literally “no way through,” for the genuine puzzlement when two equally strong arguments collide and force you to rethink the question itself. “After an hour of debate, the team hit an aporia: every fix for the bug introduced a worse one, and nobody could say which trade-off was right.”
